page: Amazon Web Services i7ie.xlarge is a storage-optimized instance powered by the AWS Nitro hypervisor. It features an x86_64 architecture with an Intel Xeon 8559C processor operating at 3.2 GHz. The instance provides 4 vCPUs (2 physical cores with hyper-threading) and a dedicated CPU allocation. It is equipped with 32.0 GB of high-speed DDR5 memory running at 6 GHz, translating to 8.0 GB of RAM per core. For local storage, the instance includes a bundled 2500 GB NVMe SSD, and it offers a baseline network bandwidth of 4 Gbps.

Performance benchmarks reveal strong single-core capabilities, with a Geekbench single-core score of 2314.0 placing it in the top 10% tier. Single-threaded tasks like gzip compression (34.74 GB/sec) and bzip3 decompression (14.0 GB/sec) perform strongly. However, multi-core performance is more modest, with a stress-ng multi-core score of 4390.57 and a Geekbench multi-core score of 5145.0, both falling into the average or weak categories due to the low core count. Memory bandwidth is relatively weak for small block reads (340.53 GB/sec) and large block reads (34.18 GB/sec), though large block writes achieve an average rating of 36.32 GB/sec.

From a qualitative cost-efficiency perspective, the i7ie.xlarge offers high storage density and memory capacity relative to its 4 vCPU compute footprint, making it a specialized choice for workloads that do not require massive parallel processing but demand substantial local NVMe storage and DDR5 memory. It is well-suited for database operations, local caching layers, and text processing tasks. However, it is less optimal for highly parallelized compute workloads, heavy multi-threaded compiling, or memory-bandwidth-bound applications.

It is equipped with 32.0 GB of DDR5 memory and a bundled 2500 GB NVMe SSD, providing high storage density and a 1:8 vCPU-to-RAM ratio. Benchmarks highlight exceptional single-core performance, with a Geekbench single-core score in the top 10% tier, alongside strong single-threaded compression and text processing capabilities. Conversely, multi-core and memory read bandwidth benchmarks are relatively weak, reflecting the physical core limit of its hardware profile. This instance is qualitatively cost-efficient for storage-heavy and memory-intensive workloads that do not require massive parallel compute, making it highly suitable for database operations, caching, and localized data processing.
